response.text:
His first lecture was his last. One hour sufficed to satisfy the young man that he had made another failure in education, and this time a fatal one. He had thought Harvard a torpid school, but it was instinct with life compared with the University of Berlin. In the Civil Law he found only the lecture system in its deadliest form as it flourished in the thirteenth century: the professor mumbled; the students made notes; they could have learned more from books in a day than from him in a month. To an American the result was worthless.

The students themselves never pretended to take their professor seriously. They were much more serious in reading Heine. They knew no more than Heine what good they were getting, beyond the Berlin accent—which was bad; the beer—which was not to compare with Munich; and the dancing—which was better at Vienna. Anyway, they were learning the language.

So the young man fell back on the language, and being slow at it, fell behind his friends—the more depressing because the gloom of a Berlin winter and of Berlin architecture seemed to him a particular sort of gloom never attained elsewhere. Once on the Linden he caught sight of Charles Sumner in a cab, then recovering from the South Carolinian cane, and ran after him; Sumner tried to encourage him with assurances of his own past mastery. A Boston acquaintance suggested a more desperate course: enter a public school and sit with ten-year-old boys, catching their phrases. He attended the Friedrichs-Wilhelm-Werdersches Gymnasium as a member of the Ober-tertia, a class of boys twelve or thirteen years old. He never did anything else so foolish, but he was given a bit of education which served him some purpose in life.

He had revolted at the American school and university; he had instantly rejected the German university; and as his last experience of education he tried the German high school. In 1858 Berlin was a poor, keen-witted, provincial town, simple, dirty, uncivilized, and in most respects disgusting. As an episode in the search for education, this adventure smacked of Heine. The arbitrary training given to the memory was stupefying; the strain a form of torture. No other faculty than the memory seemed to be recognized. Least of all was any use made of reason. The German government did not encourage reasoning.

All State education is a sort of dynamo machine for polarizing the popular mind; for turning and holding its lines of force in the direction supposed to be most effective for State purposes. The German machine was terribly efficient. Apparently Adams, in his rigidly illogical pursuit, had at last reached his ideal of a viciously logical education. The boys' physique showed it: white faces, flabby flesh, foul air in tightly closed rooms; when the American opened a window in the five minutes between hours, he violated the rules and was invariably rebuked. The German university had seemed a failure, but the German high school was something very near an indictable nuisance.

Before April arrived, the experiment of German education had reached its end. Yet by-products turn out to be more valuable than staples. The student's only clear gain—his single step to a higher life—came from time wasted, studies neglected, vices indulged; it came from the despised beer-garden and music-hall; and it was accidental, unintended, unforeseen.

Sitting at his beer-table among fat German Haus-frauen, mentally impassive while an orchestra played, Adams was one day surprised to notice that his mind followed the movement of a Sinfonie. He could not have been more astonished had he suddenly read a new language. A prison-wall that barred his senses on one great side of life suddenly fell, of its own accord, without so much as his knowing when it happened. Amid the fumes of coarse tobacco and poor beer, a new sense burst out like a flower in his life, so superior to the old senses, so bewildering, that he watched it as something apart, accidental, and not to be trusted. Beethoven had partly become intelligible to him, though he inclined the more to think Beethoven must be much overrated, to be so easily followed. Mere mechanical repetition of certain sounds had stuck to his unconscious mind.

No other sense awoke. His sense of line and color remained as dull as ever; his metaphysical sense did not spring into life; he shed never a tear over Goethe and Schiller. Yet when April came, and some genius suggested a tramp in Thüringen, his heart sang like a bird; he realized what a nightmare he had suffered, and made up his mind that, wherever else he might seek for education, it should not be again in Berlin.
